title: Abortion & the Unborn
desc: Passages cited in discussions about personhood, life, and the status of the unborn.

verses.note: God knitting a person together in the womb — widely cited for the personhood of the unborn.
God knowing and appointing Jeremiah before birth — used to argue for prenatal personhood.
John the Baptist leaping in the womb at Mary's greeting — cited for fetal awareness and personhood.
Injury to a pregnant woman — the legal status of the unborn has been debated extensively from this text.
'Sinful from conception' — cited for personhood beginning at conception.
Life begins when God breathes breath into the nostrils — cited by some as marking the start of personhood at birth.
A priest-administered test that could end a pregnancy — cited in debates about how the OT law treated fetal life.
Job cursing the day of his birth and mourning stillbirths — cited in discussions of fetal life and personhood.
The Servant called from the womb — another prenatal calling passage.
'Rescue those being led away to death' — cited in arguments about speaking for the vulnerable.

title: Homosexuality
desc: Passages cited across traditions in discussions about same-sex relationships.

verses.note: Male and female created in God's image, blessed and called to multiply — cited for male-female as the created norm.
Man and woman united as one flesh — cited as the foundational definition of marriage.
Male same-sex intercourse prohibited — the primary Levitical text; context and application debated.
Paul describes same-sex relations as contrary to nature — the most discussed NT text on this topic.
A list including arsenokoitai and malakoi — translation and meaning of these terms is actively debated.
Jesus defines marriage with reference to Genesis male/female — cited for the traditional view.
The men of Sodom — whether the sin was sexual violence, inhospitality, or homosexuality specifically is debated.
Sodom's sin described as pride and neglect of the poor — cited by those who question a primarily sexual reading.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — cited in affirming arguments about the inclusivity of the new covenant.
'What God has made clean, do not call unclean' — cited in some affirming arguments about moral revision.

title: Gender Identity
desc: Passages cited in discussions about biological sex, gender, and identity.

verses.note: 'Male and female he created them' — the primary text cited for the binary nature of biological sex.
Prohibition on cross-dressing — cited in traditional arguments; applicability to gender identity is debated.
'Fearfully and wonderfully made' — cited both for the goodness of embodiment and for affirmation of gender diverse experience.
Jesus references 'male and female at the beginning' — cited for the creational norm of binary sex.
Eunuchs given 'a name better than sons and daughters' — cited in affirming arguments about gender non-conformity.
'Eunuchs born that way' — cited by some as acknowledging biological sex variations.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — cited for the diminished significance of gender distinctions in the new covenant.
'New creation' in Christ — cited in arguments about identity being redefined by the gospel.
Body as temple of the Holy Spirit — cited in discussions about the significance of the body.

title: Marriage & Divorce
desc: What Scripture says about the nature, purpose, and dissolution of marriage.

verses.note: The first marriage — used as the template for marriage across the traditions.
Jesus on divorce: allows it for sexual immorality (πορνεία), affirms the original creational design.
Paul on marriage, celibacy, and divorce — includes the 'Pauline privilege' for mixed marriages.
Husband and wife as a picture of Christ and the church — foundational but interpretation of roles is widely debated.
'God hates divorce' — a strong statement requiring context; the exact Hebrew is also debated.
Romantic and erotic love celebrated as God's good gift within covenant relationship.
'Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure.'
Paul commends singleness as freeing one for undivided devotion to God.
The capable wife — a poem celebrating a woman of strength and dignity, not passivity.

title: Slavery
desc: The Bible's complex engagement with slavery — from regulation to liberation.

verses.note: Hebrew slave laws — provide rights and release, but also permit certain forms of bondservitude.
'Do not return a runaway slave' — remarkable protection for escaped slaves in the ancient world.
'Enslavers' (ἀνδραποδισταῖς) listed among the lawless — cited as a condemnation of slave-trading.
Paul's letter urging Philemon to receive Onesimus as a 'dear brother' — the seed of abolition in the NT.
'Neither slave nor free in Christ' — cited as undermining slavery's fundamental premise.
Instructions to slaves and masters — cited both to justify and to critique slavery, depending on the reading.
'If you can gain your freedom, do so' — Paul encouraging slaves to seek freedom when possible.
Kidnapping someone for enslavement is punishable by death — cited against the Atlantic slave trade.
Fellow Israelites not to be treated as slaves — a principle with wider implications.

title: End Times & Eschatology
desc: Passages central to the major views on what happens at the end of history.

verses.note: The Olivet Discourse — Jesus's teaching on the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the age; fulfilled vs. future readings debated.
The 'rapture' passage — believers caught up to meet the Lord; pre/mid/post-tribulation debates center here.
The thousand-year reign — the key text dividing pre-, post-, and amillennialists.
The 70 weeks — one of the most interpreted prophetic passages; various 'gap' and 'no gap' readings exist.
The Day of the LORD and the new heavens and earth — annihilation or renewal of the cosmos?
The new creation — wolves and lambs together; cited by premillennialists for a literal future kingdom.
'He will come back in the same way you have seen him go' — the bodily return of Christ.
Apocalyptic battle at Jerusalem — interpreted literally by some, symbolically by others.
'Some standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming' — fuels preterist readings.
New Jerusalem descending from heaven — the goal of all history; God dwells with humanity.

title: Predestination & Free Will
desc: The great debate between divine sovereignty and human responsibility.

verses.note: 'Foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified' — the golden chain of Calvinist soteriology.
Chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world — foundational for Reformed election theology.
'No one can come to me unless the Father draws them' — cited for unconditional election.
Jacob and Esau, the potter and clay — Paul's strongest argument for God's sovereign choice.
'As many as were appointed to eternal life believed' — a key Calvinist proof text.
God is 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' — central to Arminian arguments.
'Whoever believes' — the open invitation of the gospel cited for human responsibility.
God desires all people to be saved — cited for universal salvific will.
'Let the one who desires take the water of life without price' — the open invitation.
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked — cited for genuine divine desire for all to turn.

title: The Trinity
desc: Passages foundational to Trinitarian theology and debates about God's nature.

verses.note: Baptism in 'the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit' — one name, three persons; foundational Trinitarian text.
'The Word was God' — the full deity of the Son; Arians translate 'a god,' Trinitarians 'God.'
'The Father and I are one' — unity of essence claimed by Trinitarians; others read it as functional unity.
'Let us make man in our image' — the plural debated as royal plural, angels, or intra-Trinitarian address.
The child called 'Mighty God, Everlasting Father' — applied to Jesus in NT; key Trinitarian text.
'The LORD our God, the LORD is one' — the Shema; the bedrock monotheism Trinitarians claim to preserve.
The Trinitarian benediction — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit coordinated as equal sources of grace.
Jesus sends 'another Helper' — the Spirit as a distinct person alongside the Son.
'In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily' — the incarnation of the full Godhead.
Jesus asking to be restored to the glory he had 'before the world existed' — pre-existence of the Son.

title: Water Baptism
desc: The mode, meaning, and necessity of baptism across Christian traditions.

verses.note: 'Go and baptize' — the command foundational to all traditions of Christian baptism.
'Repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins' — cited for baptismal regeneration.
Baptism as dying and rising with Christ — the participatory/symbolic meaning.
'Baptism now saves you' — one of the strongest baptismal regeneration texts; the parenthetical context is disputed.
'Clothed with Christ through baptism' — union with Christ through the rite.
The Spirit falls before baptism — cited by those who see baptism as a response to grace, not its vehicle.
The thief on the cross promised paradise without baptism — cited against baptism as strictly necessary.
Baptism linked to circumcision — a key text for paedobaptists (infant baptism).
John's water baptism contrasted with the Spirit baptism Jesus brings — raises questions about the two.

title: Baptism in the Holy Spirit
desc: What Spirit-baptism is, when it occurs, and whether tongues are its evidence.

verses.note: Jesus commands the disciples to wait for the baptism of the Holy Spirit — the initiating promise.
Pentecost — the Spirit poured out with tongues of fire; tongues as first sign.
The 'Gentile Pentecost' — Spirit falls on Cornelius's household with tongues before water baptism.
Samaritans receive the Spirit through the laying on of hands — a distinct second experience.
Ephesian disciples rebaptized and Spirit received with tongues and prophecy.
'By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body' — cited by those who see Spirit-baptism as conversion.
Tongues as prayer and edification — Paul's nuanced treatment of the gift.
'Rivers of living water' — referring to the Spirit not yet given; anticipates Pentecost.
'How much more will your Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask' — ongoing prayer for the Spirit.

title: Sabbath Rest
desc: Whether Christians are bound to the Sabbath, and what rest means in Christ.

verses.note: God rests on the seventh day and hallows it — the creational foundation of Sabbath.
The fourth commandment — Sabbath as covenant sign; its continuing applicability is debated.
'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' — Jesus relativizes the Sabbath institution.
Sabbath described as a 'shadow' of what was to come; its observance not required — key text for fulfilled-Sabbath view.
Each person should be 'fully convinced in their own mind' about observing days.
A 'Sabbath rest remains for the people of God' — interpreted as rest in Christ or a literal future rest.
The church meeting on the first day of the week — the basis for Sunday as the Christian gathering day.
Sabbath as delight, not burden — God's vision of joyful rest.
'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath' — Jesus's authority over the institution.

title: Tithing & Giving
desc: Whether the tithe is a binding Christian obligation or a guide for generous giving.

verses.note: 'Bring the full tithe into the storehouse' — the most-quoted tithing text; context is OT covenant.
Abraham tithing to Melchizedek before the Mosaic law — cited for tithing as a pre-law principle.
Jesus commends tithing 'mint and dill' while not neglecting justice and mercy — affirmation of tithing in principle.
'Give what you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion' — cited against mandatory tithing.
Melchizedek's tithe shows the superiority of Melchizedek's priesthood — used to argue for tithing in the new covenant.
The widow's offering — Jesus commends sacrificial giving beyond a mere percentage.
Regular proportional giving on the first day of the week — the NT giving principle.
Early church sharing everything — a model of radical generosity beyond the tithe.
'A tenth of everything from the land belongs to the LORD' — the Mosaic tithe's original context.

title: Church Leadership
desc: Who may lead, how authority works, and the shape of healthy church governance.

verses.note: Qualifications for overseers and deacons — the most detailed NT leadership criteria.
Elder qualifications for local churches — parallel to 1 Timothy 3; character-centred.
Elders to 'shepherd the flock' as undershepherds under Christ; servant leadership, not dominance.
Jesus defines greatness as servanthood — the counter-cultural leadership model.
Paul appointing elders in every church — plurality of elders as the Pauline pattern.
'I do not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man' — central to complementarian arguments.
'Neither male nor female in Christ' — central to egalitarian arguments about leadership.
Phoebe as διάκονος (deacon/minister) — evidence of women in formal church roles.
Junia 'outstanding among the apostles' — debated: was Junia an apostle, or notable to the apostles?
Priscilla (listed first) explains the way of God to Apollos — a woman teaching a man in Acts.

title: Divine Healing
desc: Whether miraculous healing is in the atonement, promised for today, and how to pray for the sick.

verses.note: 'By his stripes we are healed' — cited for healing in the atonement; Matthew applies it to Jesus's healing ministry.
Jesus heals all who are sick to 'fulfill what was spoken by Isaiah the prophet' — Matthew's application of Isaiah 53.
'Is any among you sick? Let the elders pray' — the primary NT text for healing prayer.
'By his wounds you have been healed' — Peter quotes Isaiah 53 in the context of spiritual healing (from sin).
Signs including healing will follow believers — the longer ending; text-critical issues noted.
Paul's thorn was not healed despite three prayers — cited to balance triumphalist healing theology.
Paul advises Timothy to take wine for his stomach — medical means not excluded by faith.
Epaphroditus nearly died — illness is not always rebuked or immediately healed.
Man blind from birth — Jesus says it was not due to sin; corrects the equation of suffering with faithlessness.

title: Women in Ministry
desc: A central debate: may women preach, teach, and lead in the church?

verses.note: 'Neither male nor female — all are one in Christ Jesus' — the foundational egalitarian text.
Paul does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man — the foundational complementarian text.
Women to be silent in churches — context (asking questions vs. all speech) and application are debated.
Women praying and prophesying in church — assumes women speak publicly, just with head covered.
'Your daughters will prophesy' — the Spirit's outpouring explicitly includes women as proclaimers.
Philip's four daughters were prophetesses — acknowledged female prophetic ministry.
Phoebe commended as a deacon and benefactor — evidence of a woman in formal church ministry.
Deborah as both prophet and judge of all Israel — a woman exercising the highest leadership in the OT.
The capable woman 'speaks with wisdom' and teaches — wisdom as a feminine voice in Proverbs.

title: Capital Punishment
desc: Biblical teaching on whether the state may lawfully take a life as punishment.

verses.note: 'Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed' — the foundational text for capital punishment.
Death for murder in Mosaic law — intentional vs. unintentional distinctions.
Government 'does not bear the sword in vain' — widely cited for state authority to execute.
No ransom accepted for murder — the death penalty is mandatory in the Mosaic system.
The woman caught in adultery — Jesus does not enforce the death penalty; cited for its abolition.
'You have heard eye for eye…but I say turn the other cheek' — Jesus's revision of retributive justice.
'Vengeance is mine, says the Lord' — cited for entrusting justice to God rather than human execution.
Paul acknowledges that if he deserves death, he will not resist it — implicit affirmation of the state's right.
Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent are both abominations to God.

title: Just War & Pacifism
desc: May a Christian fight? When, if ever, is war justifiable?

verses.note: Governing authorities bear the sword against evil — the primary text for Christian participation in state force.
'Blessed are the peacemakers' — the beatitude foundational to pacifist ethics.
'Do not resist the evil person' — the non-resistance command at the heart of pacifism.
Soldiers told to be content with their pay, not to quit the army — John the Baptist does not condemn military service.
'Greater love has no one than to lay down his life for his friends' — cited for soldiers' sacrifice.
'They will beat their swords into plowshares' — the eschatological vision of universal peace.
'A time for war and a time for peace' — cited for the legitimacy of war in a fallen world.
Jesus tells the disciples to buy swords — variously interpreted as literal, symbolic, or a limited provision.
Christ himself returns as a warrior king — cited for just-war theology's divine legitimacy.

title: Alcohol & Sobriety
desc: From wine at Cana to warnings about drunkenness — what the Bible says about drinking.

verses.note: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding — and the headwaiter praises its quality; cited for moderate drinking.
'Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler' — a strong warning against alcohol's dangers.
'Do not get drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit' — the NT's clearest prohibition of drunkenness.
Paul tells Timothy to drink a little wine for his stomach — medicinal use of wine affirmed.
'Give wine to those who are bitter in soul' — wine as comfort for the suffering; not absolute prohibition.
It is good not to drink wine if it causes a brother to stumble — conscience and community over personal freedom.
The Nazirite vow requires abstaining from all wine — total abstinence as a form of holy consecration.
Drunkenness listed among the works of the flesh that exclude from God's kingdom.
'Wine that gladdens human hearts' — creation's gift; God's good provision for joy.

title: Wealth & Poverty
desc: Does God promise prosperity? How should Christians relate to money?

verses.note: 'Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom' — Jesus's radical warning.
'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' — not money itself, but love of it.
The rich fool who stored up earthly goods but was not rich toward God.
Rich man and Lazarus — the reversal of fortune after death; a warning against indifference to the poor.
'Weep and howl, you rich people' — James's most severe address to the wealthy who exploit workers.
'Lazy hands make for poverty' — work and diligence as paths to provision.
'God loves a cheerful giver' and will make grace abound for generous giving.
The early church held everything in common and distributed to any who had need.
'Do not say to yourself, my power produced this wealth' — God gives the ability to produce wealth.
'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD' — generosity to the poor is generosity to God.
